title: why bow three times?
hookLine: palms together, forehead to the floor, three times: who the bows are for, and why the incense
carry: bow to what wakes you up

cards: Shoes off at the door. Palms together. Then down: knees, hands, forehead to the floor.
Up. Again. And a third time.
If you grew up going to temple, your body may know this before your mind ever asked why. Seen from outside, in a film or a yoga studio, it can look like worshiping a statue. It isn't quite that.
The clue is the number three.

teach.h: THE BUDDHA — ONE WHO WOKE UP
teach.b: Each bow has a name, and together Buddhists call them the three jewels. The first is the Buddha: not a god, but a person who woke up. Many teachers say the bow is to that possibility of waking up, in anyone.
The second is the Dharma, Dhamma in Pali: the teaching, and the way things actually are.
The third is the Sangha: the community that practices it, monks and nuns, and in many places everyone walking the path together.
Before chanting, many Buddhists say they go for refuge to these three, in Pali: Buddham saranam gacchami, I go to the Buddha for refuge, and so on for the other two.
So the statue is a reminder, a bit like a photo of someone you love.

teach.h: INCENSE — RESPECT, NOT FOOD FOR A GOD

teach.b: At a Buddhist altar it's offered as respect, not as something a god needs. One old verse says the scent of flowers only travels with the wind, but the goodness of a person travels even against it.

how: At a temple or home shrine, many Buddhists bow three times, palms together, often touching knees, hands and forehead to the floor, to the Buddha, the Dharma and the Sangha; many light incense and recite the three refuges, Buddham saranam gacchami, before chanting.

games.q: what's inside the bows — tap the pairs.
p: the teaching, and how things are
respect, not something a god needs

s: a Buddhist bowing to a statue is worshiping it as a god
the three bows go to the Buddha, the teaching and the community. many teachers call the statue a reminder.
the three bows match the three jewels
one each for the Buddha, the Dharma and the Sangha.
Buddham saranam gacchami means I go to the Buddha for refuge
it's said three times, once for each jewel, in many temples.

games.q: an old verse compares the scent of flowers with the goodness of a person. which one travels even against the wind?
games.why: flowers and sandalwood only carry with the wind. the verse says a good person's fragrance spreads in every direction.

games.q: put the three bows in order.

practice: One breath with the bell. Bring your palms together at your chest, if you like. Breathe in.
As you breathe out, tip your head forward, just slightly: a small bow to whatever in you is trying to wake up.

wordCard.voice: The three jewels. The Buddha, the Dharma and the Sangha: the one who woke up, the teaching, and the people who walk it. Second word.

orig.note: Pali: the three jewels. ti, three; ratana, jewel. Sanskrit: triratna.

carryVoice: Your line: bow to what wakes you up. Three bows, and none of them is to a statue. Day two, done.
